items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the economic development law, in relation to establishing the
transitional green development program
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S783

SPONSOR: BRESLIN
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the economic development law, in relation to establish-
ing the transitional green development program

 
PURPOSE:

Creates the Transitional Green Development Grant Program to assist
upstate communities with declining industrial bases to identify and
coordinate their natural, cultural and historical resources into a stra-
tegic, sustainable development plan.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 provides legislative findings.

Section 2 adds a new Article 23 to the Economic Development Law(§§ 450
through 454) creating the Transitional Green Development Grant Program.

§ 450 provides definitions, whereby: "Transitional Green Development"
means utilizing all elements of a municipality's current cultural,
educational, environmental and infrastructural character, and coordinat-
ing those attributes with vestiges of its industrial past to achieve
sustainable green development; the "Transitional Green Development Coor-
dinator" means an individual designated by the executive of the munici-
pality to identify community resources, and direct, coordinate and
develop a plan for transitional green development; "Transitional Green
Development Grant" is a two-year grant, not to exceed $150,000, funded
through the Empire State Development Corporation, to bring together a
wide range of community partners in a collaborative effort to identify
the municipality's unique qualities, and design strategies to best
exploit those characteristics for sustainable green development.

§ 451 establishes the Transitional Green Development Program

§ 452 provides for the distribution and acceptable uses for the grants.

§ 453 provides for the duties and responsibilities of the Transitional
Green Development Coordinator.

§ 454 provides that the Commissioner of Economic Development will
promulgate rules and regulations to implement the program.

Section 2 of the bill is the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Many of the State's formerly industrial cities have been reeling from
the loss of their manufacturing base for decades, and are struggling to
redefine themselves in their post-industrial reality. Most of them have
special features - such as historic properties, waterfront areas, muse-
ums, educational facilities or even former manufacturing buildings that
can be redefined and exploited as economic assets with great potential
to spark redevelopment and grow jobs.(1) For instance, according to a
study by the Brookings Institute, just twelve of New York's former
industrial areas (2) together have over 450 buildings on the National
Registry of Historic Places, 40 museums, 57 two- and four-year colleges
and universities, and 45 hospitals and medical facilities.(3) Recent and
in-progress revitalization efforts show the promise of redevelopment and
revitalization in upstate New York. Syracuse has pursued a comprehensive
redevelopment program that includes a thoughtful focus on its downtown,
including a focus on leveraging existing cultural institutions in a
planned downtown cultural district.(4) The City of Beacon has seen
increased economic activity following development of museum resources
and an effort to strengthen surrounding areas.(5) Redevelopment projects
in Buffalo have focused on repurposing formerly abandoned grain silos as
hubs for cultural, marketing and recreational activity.(6) And city
planners in Utica, in collaboration with Cornell University's comprehen-
sive "Rust to Green" (R2G) initiative, have begun redirecting and repur-
posing the City's existing cultural, infrastructural, natural and
historical resources toward a postindustrial, environmentally stable
future.(7) Many cities still, however, face budgetary constraints that
severely restrict their ability to identify their many, sometimes
obscure, resources and weave them into a sustainable, multifaceted
development strategy. This legislation establishes the Transitional
Green Development Grant Program to provide grants of up to $150,000 over
a two-year period to hire a temporary development coordinator, whose
task will be to work with community leaders to identify those resources,
develop and assist in the implementation of a Transitional Green Devel-
opment Plan.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2017-18: S.2691 Referred to Commerce, Economic Development and Small
Business

2015-16: S.6276 Referred to Commerce, Economic Development and Small
Business

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

$2 million appropriation over two years.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.
(1) Vey, J., The Brookings Institution Metropolitan Policy Program,
Restoring Prosperity: The State Role in Revitalizing America's Older
Industrial Cities (2007) at 4, 34-38.
(2) Albany, Binghamton, Buffalo, Rochester, Schenectady, Syracuse,
Utica, Elmira, Jamestown, Niagara Falls, Rome, and Troy.
(3) Brookings, Restoring Prosperity, State Profile: New York, available
at http://www.brookings.edu /-/media/Research/Files/Reports
/2007/5/metropolitanpolicyvey /20070520_oicNY.PDF.
(4) See City of Syracuse Comprehensive Plan 2040. Available at
http://www.syrgov.net/uploadedFiles /Compt20Plant20amended%202013-08-1
(5) Foderaro, L. "Beacon: A City Reborn as a Haven for Art." New York
Times (Mar. 26, 2009).
(6) See, e.g., Associated Press. "Labatt Blue turns Buffalo grain silos
into tall, frosty beer ad." (Sept. 30, 2014) (describing the transforma-
tion of six silos at the former GLF grain mill into a giant six-pack of
Labatt's Blue beer cans as the area is being transformed into a brewery,
entertainment and recreation complex); Jessica Swannie, Seven Ways to
Enjoy Silo City, VisitBuffaloNiagara.com (June 10, 2015) (describing a
series of cultural and recreational events over summer 2015 at and
around the site of former industrial grain silos); Anne Neville, Silo
City about to become Drive-ln City, Buffalo News (Aug. 20, 2015).
(7) See http://www.rust2green.org/ utica background story.php.
